subsection: 4. Global issues and a justice perspective

notes.h: A justice perspective on global issues
notes.b: Global issues are problems that cross borders and affect the whole world, such as poverty, inequality, trade rules, debt, climate change and migration. A justice perspective asks whether the distribution of wealth and power is fair, who decides, and who benefits. It treats development as a matter of rights, not charity.
points: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights, adopted by the UN General Assembly on 10 December 1948, includes rights to food, health, education and decent work.
Poverty denies these rights, so a justice perspective treats poverty as a rights failure rather than a matter of charity.
About 700 million people lived in extreme poverty in 2022, most of them in sub-Saharan Africa. The World Bank measures extreme poverty as living on under $2.15 a day (2017 prices).
The share of the world's population in extreme poverty fell from over a third in 1990 to under a tenth by 2019.
The richest 10% own about 76% of global wealth, while the poorest half own about 2% (World Inequality Report 2022).
The Millennium Development Goals (2000–2015) had eight goals. The target of halving the share of people in extreme poverty from 1990 was met by 2010, five years early, largely thanks to China.
The Sustainable Development Goals were adopted by the UN in September 2015. They have 17 goals, to be met by 2030.

The SDGs target poverty (SDG 1), hunger (SDG 2), quality education (SDG 4), gender equality (SDG 5), reduced inequalities (SDG 10) and climate action (SDG 13). Other targets cover health, clean water and climate.
The world is off track to meet most SDG targets by 2030.

notes.h: Unfair trade: commodities and the value chain
points: Many developing countries depend on exporting a few primary commodities, such as coffee, cocoa, cotton and minerals, whose prices are low and unstable.
The terms of trade tend to move against these countries, so their exports buy fewer imports over time while they import manufactured goods.
Most of the final price of coffee, chocolate or clothing goes to processors, brands and retailers in rich countries. The grower receives a small share.
Tariff escalation: rich countries charge higher tariffs on processed goods than on raw materials, which discourages poor countries from processing their own crops.

notes.h: Unfair trade: farm subsidies and the cotton case
points: Rich-country farm subsidies, such as US cotton subsidies and the EU's Common Agricultural Policy in the past, let surpluses be sold cheaply abroad. This is called dumping, and it undercuts poor farmers.
The Cotton-4 West African producers, Benin, Burkina Faso, Chad and Mali, were harmed by these subsidies.
The WTO ruled in Brazil's favour against US cotton subsidies in 2004–05.
The WTO Doha Development Round was launched in 2001 but has stalled without agreement.
The EU's 'Everything But Arms' scheme (2001) gives the least developed countries duty-free and quota-free access to the EU for all products except arms and ammunition.

notes.b: Fair trade is a trading model in which producers receive guaranteed terms and the Fairtrade Mark identifies certified products.
points: The Fairtrade Minimum Price covers the cost of sustainable production. It is a guaranteed floor, not a guaranteed higher price: when the market price is higher, producers receive the market price plus the premium.
The Fairtrade Premium is paid to producer co-operatives for community projects such as schools, clinics and clean water.
Fair trade also requires long-term contracts, decent working conditions, no child labour, environmental standards and democratically run co-operatives.
Fair trade covers coffee, tea, cocoa, bananas, sugar and cotton.
The first fair trade label, Max Havelaar, was launched in the Netherlands in 1988 for Mexican coffee. Fairtrade International now coordinates the Fairtrade Mark.

notes.h: Fair trade in Ireland and its limits
points: Fairtrade Ireland (Fairtrade Mark Ireland) licenses the Fairtrade Mark in Ireland.
Irish towns and schools can apply for Fairtrade status. Fairtrade Fortnight takes place each year in late February and March.
Fair trade makes up only a tiny share of world trade.
Certified products can cost consumers more, and certification is expensive for small producers.
Fair trade does not change the trade rules that cause unfair trade in the first place.
When oil prices rose sharply, oil-exporting countries deposited their surplus money in banks. Banks lent these deposits, called petrodollars, to developing countries.
Interest rates then rose sharply and commodity prices fell, so many borrowers could not afford repayments.
Mexico announced in August 1982 that it could not pay its debts, starting the Latin American debt crisis.
Many African and Latin American countries could not repay their debts.

notes.h: Debt: effects and the justice argument
points: Governments spent more on debt repayments than on health and education.
Countries took new loans to repay old ones, so the debt grew.
The 1980s 'lost decade' hit Latin America and Africa hard.
Some debts were 'odious': dictators borrowed the money and stole or wasted it, yet the people were made to repay it.

IMF and World Bank loans came with conditions. These cut public spending, introduced school and health fees, privatised state firms, removed food subsidies, devalued the currency and opened markets to imports.
Structural adjustment programmes were criticised for hurting the poorest people most (see Case study of a developing economy).
The Jubilee 2000 campaign pressed for debt cancellation by the millennium.
The Heavily Indebted Poor Countries (HIPC) Initiative was launched in 1996 by the IMF and World Bank.
The Multilateral Debt Relief Initiative (2005) followed the G8 summit at Gleneagles, Scotland, in July 2005. It was backed by the Make Poverty History campaign and the Live 8 concerts.
More than 30 countries, most in Africa, have received debt relief under HIPC, on condition that the savings go to poverty reduction.
Relief has funded results such as free primary education in some relieved countries.
Debt is rising again in the 2020s.
Emergency (humanitarian) aid responds to disasters and famines.
Long-term development aid funds projects that build lasting capacity.
Bilateral aid passes from one government to another.
Multilateral aid is channelled through bodies such as the UN, the World Bank and the EU.
NGO (voluntary) aid is given by non-governmental organisations.
Tied aid must be spent on goods or services from the donor country.
The UN target, set in 1970, is that rich countries give 0.7% of their gross national income as official development aid.
Norway, Sweden, Luxembourg and Denmark have reached or exceeded the target in recent years.
Ireland has not yet reached the target (2020s).
Helps: aid saves lives in emergencies and funds schools, clinics, wells and vaccination programmes.
Helps: aid builds roads and infrastructure, trains teachers, nurses and farmers, and supports women's groups and small businesses.
Hinders: tied aid benefits donor firms and may supply unsuitable technology.
Hinders: corrupt elites can steal aid, and food aid can undercut local farmers.
Hinders: aid can create dependency instead of self-reliance, and loans add to debt.
Hinders: donors' political or strategic interests decide who gets aid, rather than need.
Hinders: large prestige projects, such as dams, can displace people.
Better aid is untied, targeted at the poorest, and designed with local participation and ownership. It supports self-help and co-operatives and is transparent.
Irish Aid is Ireland's official aid programme, part of the Department of Foreign Affairs. Its bilateral programme began in 1974.
Long-term partner countries include Ethiopia, Malawi, Mozambique, Tanzania, Uganda and Zambia in sub-Saharan Africa, and Vietnam.
Ireland's aid is untied.
'A Better World' (2019), Ireland's international development policy, focuses on the furthest behind, gender equality, climate and governance.
Concern Worldwide was founded in 1968 in response to the famine in Biafra during Nigeria's civil war.
Trócaire was founded in 1973 by the Irish Catholic bishops. Its Lenten 'Trócaire box' raises funds, and it campaigns on human rights and climate.
GOAL was founded in 1977 by John O'Shea.
Live Aid concerts in July 1985, organised by Bob Geldof, responded to the 1984–85 Ethiopian famine.
The Great Famine (1845–49) killed about 1 million people and led about 1 million to emigrate. This history is one reason for Irish solidarity with developing countries.
Multinationals locate labour-intensive work, such as clothing, electronics assembly and mining, in low-wage countries.
Benefits for workers include jobs, wages higher than farm work, and skills.
Exploitation includes very low wages, long hours, unsafe factories, banned trade unions and child labour.
Rana Plaza, an eight-storey building in Savar near Dhaka, housed garment factories. It collapsed on 24 April 2013, killing about 1,130 people and injuring about 2,500.
Cracks had appeared the day before, but workers were ordered back in.
The factories supplied Western brands, including Primark, which was founded in Dublin in 1969 as Penneys. Primark paid compensation to the victims.
The Accord on Fire and Building Safety in Bangladesh was signed in May 2013 by global brands and trade unions, and eventually more than 200 brands joined. It provided independent factory inspections.
Garments make up over four-fifths of Bangladesh's exports (2020s).
The case shows how brands profit from low-cost factories while the safety of workers depends on local suppliers.
About 160 million children were in child labour worldwide in 2020 (ILO and UNICEF), about 70% of them in agriculture.
Child labour occurs in cocoa farming and in mining.
The DR Congo produces about 70% of the world's cobalt, which is used in rechargeable batteries.
Amnesty International (2016) documented child labour in the artisanal, hand-dug cobalt mines of the DR Congo.
Foreign companies and governments buy or lease large areas of farmland in poor countries, a practice called land grabbing.
Indigenous peoples lose land to mining, ranching and logging, as in the Amazon example in the Brazil section of Case study of a developing economy.
Ethical consumer campaigns and company codes of conduct put pressure on brands.
The EU Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive, adopted in 2024, requires very large companies to identify and address human-rights and environmental harm in their supply chains.
Trade unions represent workers and campaign for safer conditions and better wages.
The poorest countries have contributed least to greenhouse gas emissions but suffer most from climate change.
Bangladesh is a low-lying delta vulnerable to cyclones, floods and sea-level rise.
Small island states such as Tuvalu, Kiribati and the Maldives are threatened by sea-level rise.
Sub-Saharan Africa has produced only a small share of historical emissions, yet its dry regions suffer drought.
Responses include climate finance from rich countries and the Loss and Damage Fund, agreed at COP27 in Sharm el-Sheikh, Egypt (2022) and made operational at COP28 in Dubai (2023).
The Mary Robinson Foundation – Climate Justice was set up in 2010 by Mary Robinson, who was President of Ireland from 1990 to 1997 and UN High Commissioner for Human Rights from 1997 to 2002.
Extreme poverty has fallen greatly since 1990, especially in China. Child mortality has fallen, and more children attend school.
Sub-Saharan Africa lags behind other regions.
Inequality within and between countries is high.
Conflict, such as the war in Sudan (see Case study of a developing economy), and climate change are reversing gains.
The COVID-19 pandemic in 2020 caused the first rise in global extreme poverty in about a generation (World Bank).

notes.h: What individuals and Ireland can do
points: Individuals can buy fair trade, campaign, and support NGOs. Ireland can press governments on aid, trade and debt policy.

keyTerms.definition: A problem that crosses borders and affects the whole world, such as poverty, trade rules, debt or climate change.
The relationship between the prices a country receives for its exports and the prices it pays for its imports.
The stages from raw material to final product, and the share of the final price each stage receives.
Selling surplus goods abroad at low prices, often because of subsidies, which undercuts producers in the importing country.
A guaranteed floor price for certified producers, covering the cost of sustainable production.
An extra payment to producer co-operatives for community projects such as schools, clinics and clean water.
Oil-exporters' deposits in banks, which the banks lent on to developing countries in the 1970s.
The Heavily Indebted Poor Countries initiative, launched in 1996, which cancelled much of the debt of the poorest countries on condition that savings go to poverty reduction.
Aid that must be spent on goods or services from the donor country.
Aid that the recipient can spend on goods and services from any country.
Foreign companies or governments buying or leasing large areas of farmland in poor countries.
A fund agreed at COP27 to help poor countries pay for losses and damage caused by climate change.

factCards.term: Global extreme poverty: figure, trend since 1990 and setbacks
factCards.definition: About 700 million people (under $2.15 a day, 2017 prices) in 2022, mostly in sub-Saharan Africa. The share fell from over a third in 1990 to under a tenth by 2019, especially in China; COVID-19 in 2020 caused the first rise in about a generation (World Bank).

factCards.term: A justice perspective: what it asks, and its human-rights basis
factCards.definition: It asks whether the distribution of wealth and power is fair, who decides and who benefits, treating development as a right, not charity. The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (10 December 1948) includes rights to food, health, education and decent work.

factCards.term: MDGs and SDGs: number of goals, dates and progress
factCards.definition: MDGs: eight goals, 2000 to 2015; halving the extreme-poverty share (from 1990) was met by 2010, five years early, largely thanks to China. SDGs: 17 goals adopted in September 2015 for 2030, e.g. no poverty, zero hunger, climate action; the world is off track.

factCards.term: Unfair trade: three ways poor exporters lose out
factCards.definition: They depend on a few commodities (coffee, cocoa, cotton) with low, unstable prices and worsening terms of trade; growers get a small share of the final price, most going to rich-country brands and retailers; tariff escalation discourages local processing.

factCards.term: Rich-country farm subsidies: the cotton example
factCards.definition: US cotton subsidies (and the EU's Common Agricultural Policy in the past) let surpluses be dumped abroad, undercutting poor farmers such as the Cotton-4: Benin, Burkina Faso, Chad and Mali. The WTO ruled for Brazil against US cotton subsidies (2004–05).

factCards.term: Two trade responses: the Doha Round and Everything But Arms
factCards.definition: The WTO Doha Development Round, launched in 2001, has stalled without agreement. The EU's Everything But Arms scheme (2001) gives the least developed countries duty-free, quota-free access to the EU for all products except arms and ammunition.

factCards.term: Fair trade: five ways it helps producers
factCards.definition: A minimum price covering sustainable production (or the market price plus premium when that is higher); a premium paid to co-operatives for schools, clinics and clean water; long-term contracts; decent conditions and no child labour; environmental standards.

factCards.term: Fair trade: first label, products and Irish links
factCards.definition: Max Havelaar, the first label, began in the Netherlands in 1988 for Mexican coffee. Products include coffee, cocoa and bananas. Fairtrade Ireland licenses the Mark; towns and schools win Fairtrade status; Fairtrade Fortnight runs late February to March.

factCards.term: Fair trade: four limits
factCards.definition: It is a tiny share of world trade; certified products can cost consumers more; certification is expensive for small producers; it does not change the trade rules that cause unfair trade.

factCards.term: The debt crisis: how it arose, in order
factCards.definition: 1970s oil price rises gave oil exporters surplus money, which banks lent to developing countries (petrodollars). Interest rates then soared and commodity prices fell. In August 1982 Mexico said it could not pay, starting the Latin American debt crisis.

factCards.term: Debt: effects on poor countries, and why it is unjust
factCards.definition: Repayments exceeded health and education spending: a lost decade in the 1980s. Structural adjustment cut public spending, added school and health fees and removed food subsidies, hurting the poorest. Odious debts were borrowed by dictators who stole or wasted the money, yet the people repay them.

factCards.term: Debt relief: campaigns, initiatives and results
factCards.definition: Jubilee 2000 campaigned for cancellation; the IMF and World Bank launched HIPC in 1996; the Multilateral Debt Relief Initiative followed the Gleneagles G8 summit (July 2005), backed by Make Poverty History. Over 30 countries, most in Africa, got relief.

factCards.term: Name six types of aid
factCards.definition: Emergency (humanitarian) aid after disasters; long-term development aid; bilateral, government to government; multilateral, through the UN, World Bank or EU; NGO (voluntary) aid; tied aid, which must be spent on the donor's goods or services.

factCards.term: The UN aid target: what it is and who meets it
factCards.definition: Set in 1970: rich countries should give 0.7% of gross national income as official development aid. Norway, Sweden, Luxembourg and Denmark have reached or exceeded it in recent years; Ireland has not yet (2020s).

factCards.term: How aid helps development, and what makes it work best
factCards.definition: It saves lives in emergencies; funds schools, clinics, wells and vaccination; builds roads; trains teachers, nurses and farmers; supports women's groups and small businesses. It works best untied, targeted at the poorest, locally owned and transparent.

factCards.term: How aid can hinder development: five ways
factCards.definition: Tied aid benefits donor firms and may bring unsuitable technology; corrupt elites can steal it; food aid can undercut local farmers; it can create dependency, and loans add to debt; donors' political interests, not need, can decide who gets it.

factCards.term: Irish Aid: five facts
factCards.definition: Ireland's official aid programme, in the Department of Foreign Affairs; bilateral since 1974; untied; partners include Ethiopia, Malawi, Mozambique, Tanzania, Uganda, Zambia and Vietnam; A Better World (2019) puts the furthest behind first.

factCards.term: Three Irish NGOs: when each was founded, and by whom or why
factCards.definition: Concern Worldwide, 1968, in response to the famine in Biafra during Nigeria's civil war; Trócaire, 1973, by the Irish Catholic bishops, known for its Lenten box and campaigns on human rights and climate; GOAL, 1977, by John O'Shea.

factCards.term: Multinationals in low-wage countries: benefits vs exploitation
factCards.definition: They locate labour-intensive work (clothing, electronics assembly, mining) there. Benefits: jobs, wages above farm work, new skills. Exploitation: very low wages, long hours, unsafe factories, banned trade unions and child labour.

factCards.term: Rana Plaza, 2013: what happened
factCards.definition: An eight-storey building of garment factories in Savar, near Dhaka, Bangladesh, collapsed on 24 April 2013, killing about 1,130 people and injuring about 2,500. Cracks had appeared the day before, but workers were ordered back in.

factCards.term: Rana Plaza: the brands involved and the response
factCards.definition: Its factories supplied Western brands, including Primark (founded in Dublin in 1969 as Penneys), which paid compensation. In May 2013 brands and unions signed the Accord on Fire and Building Safety in Bangladesh, with independent factory inspections.

factCards.term: Child labour: global figure and the cobalt example
factCards.definition: About 160 million children were in child labour in 2020 (ILO and UNICEF), about 70% in agriculture. The DR Congo produces about 70% of the world's cobalt, used in batteries; Amnesty International (2016) documented child labour in its hand-dug mines.

factCards.term: Four responses to the exploitation of workers
factCards.definition: Ethical consumer campaigns; company codes of conduct; trade unions pressing for safer, better-paid work; the EU Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (2024), making very large companies address human-rights and environmental harm in supply chains.

factCards.term: Climate justice: who emits least but suffers most
factCards.definition: Bangladesh, a low-lying delta, faces cyclones, floods and sea-level rise; Tuvalu, Kiribati and the Maldives are threatened by rising seas; sub-Saharan Africa produced only a small share of historical emissions yet its dry regions suffer drought.

factCards.term: Climate justice: two responses with names and dates
factCards.definition: The Loss and Damage Fund, agreed at COP27 in Sharm el-Sheikh, Egypt (2022), made operational at COP28 in Dubai (2023); the Mary Robinson Foundation – Climate Justice (2010), set up by the former President of Ireland (1990–97).

questions.prompt: Discuss two global justice issues relating to uneven levels of economic development.
questions.model: Unfair trade is one global justice issue. Many developing countries depend on exporting a few primary commodities such as coffee, cocoa, cotton and minerals, whose prices are low and unstable, while they import manufactured goods, so the terms of trade tend to move against them. Most of the final price of coffee or chocolate goes to processors, brands and retailers in rich countries, while growers receive a small share. Rich countries charge higher tariffs on processed goods than on raw materials, which discourages processing in poor countries. Rich-country farm subsidies, such as US cotton subsidies, let surpluses be sold cheaply abroad as dumping, undercutting West African cotton growers, and the WTO ruled against those US subsidies in 2004–05 in Brazil's favour. Responses include the stalled WTO Doha Development Round and the EU's Everything But Arms scheme, and fair trade, which guarantees a minimum price and pays a premium for community projects. Its limits are that it covers only a tiny share of world trade, certified products can cost consumers more, and it does not change the trade rules. Debt is a second justice issue. Oil-price rises led banks to lend petrodollars to developing countries, and when interest rates rose and commodity prices fell, Mexico announced in August 1982 that it could not pay, starting the Latin American debt crisis. Debt repayments took more money than health and education, and the 1980s lost decade followed. IMF and World Bank structural adjustment conditions such as cuts to public spending and school and health fees hurt the poorest. Some debts were odious, yet the people were made to repay them. Relief came through Jubilee 2000, the HIPC Initiative launched in 1996 and the Multilateral Debt Relief Initiative of 2005, which freed money for poverty reduction, but debt is rising again in the 2020s.

questions.prompt: Examine how aid can both help and hinder development, with reference to examples you have studied.
questions.model: Aid comes in several types: emergency aid after disasters and famines, long-term development aid, bilateral aid between governments, multilateral aid through bodies such as the UN, the World Bank and the EU, NGO aid, and tied aid, which must be spent on the donor's goods and services. Aid helps in several ways. It saves lives in emergencies, funds schools, clinics, wells and vaccination programmes, trains teachers, nurses and farmers, and supports women's groups and small businesses. Aid can also hinder development. Tied aid benefits donor firms and may supply unsuitable technology, and corrupt elites can steal it. Food aid can undercut local farmers, and aid can create dependency rather than self-reliance. Loans add to debt, and donors' political or strategic interests can decide who gets aid rather than need. Large prestige projects such as dams can displace people. Irish Aid is Ireland's official aid programme, part of the Department of Foreign Affairs. Its aid is untied, and its long-term partners are mainly in sub-Saharan Africa, including Ethiopia, Malawi, Mozambique, Tanzania, Uganda and Zambia, and Vietnam. Concern Worldwide, founded in 1968 in response to the Biafra famine, is an Irish NGO that works on emergencies and long-term development. Aid is more effective when it is untied, targeted at the poorest, designed with local participation and ownership, supports self-help and co-operatives, and is transparent.

questions.prompt: Explain how fair trade helps producers in developing countries.
questions.model: Fair trade helps producers by guaranteeing a Fairtrade Minimum Price that covers the cost of sustainable production, so growers are protected when world prices fall. Producers also receive the Fairtrade Premium, a payment to their co-operatives for community projects such as schools, clinics and clean water. Producers are organised in democratic co-operatives, which gives them a voice in how money is spent. Fair trade requires long-term contracts, decent working conditions and no child labour, and it sets environmental standards. Products carry the Fairtrade Mark, which Fairtrade International coordinates. In Ireland, Fairtrade Ireland licenses the Fairtrade Mark, and Irish towns and schools can apply for Fairtrade status during Fairtrade Fortnight in late February and March. One limit is that fair trade covers only a tiny share of world trade, so its benefits reach few producers.
